questions.prompt: Why does Swift's assignment operator `=` not return a value, and what bug does this prevent? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: States that assignment does not return a value (returns Void) in Swift
Explains that it stops accidental assignment inside if conditions
Contrasts with languages like C where if (x = y) compiles

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, the assignment operator `=` returns Void instead of returning the assigned value. This design stops programmers from writing assignment by mistake when they mean to check equality inside conditions. In languages like C, writing `if (x = y)` assigns y to x and compiles without error. In Swift, writing `if x = y` fails to compile right away.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Basic Operators

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between value equality `==` and reference identity `===` in Swift. Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Defines == as checking whether two values have equal data
Defines === as checking whether two references point to the same class instance
States that === only works on class instances, not value types like structs

questions.modelAnswer: The `==` operator tests value equality by checking whether two values have equal data. The `===` operator tests reference identity. It checks whether two references point to the exact same class instance in memory. Because structs and enums are value types without reference identity, `===` only applies to class instances.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Basic Operators

questions.prompt: Compare the closed range operator `a...b` and the half-open range operator `a..<b`. Give one use case for each. Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that closed range includes both ends a and b
Explains that half-open range leaves out the upper bound b
Gives one clear use case for each range type

questions.modelAnswer: The closed range operator `a...b` includes both ends from a through b. It works well for full number spans, such as days `1...31`. The half-open range operator `a..<b` runs from a up to b without including b. It works well for arrays that start at index 0, such as looping over `0..<items.count`.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Basic Operators

questions.prompt: How does short-circuit evaluation work in Swift's nil-coalescing operator `??`, and why is this useful? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: States that the right side only runs when the left optional is nil
Explains that if the left side has a value, the right side is skipped
Notes that skipping the right side avoids extra work or side effects

questions.modelAnswer: The nil-coalescing operator `??` uses short-circuit evaluation. When the optional on the left has a value, Swift unwraps it and skips the expression on the right. The right side only runs if the optional is nil. This avoids extra work, slow calls, or side effects when a value already exists.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Basic Operators

questions.prompt: What happens when a standard math operation overflows an integer type in Swift? How does Swift differ from C in this behavior? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: States that Swift traps with a runtime crash on integer overflow
Contrasts with C where overflow wraps silently or is undefined behavior
Mentions that overflow operators like &+ are used when wrapping is wanted

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, standard math operators check for overflow by default. If a number goes past its type limits, Swift stops the app with a crash. In C, integer overflow can wrap silently or cause undefined behavior, which leads to hard bugs. When you actually want wrapping in Swift, you use overflow operators such as `&+` or `&*`.
